imc-1999-01.title: Eigenvalues are roots of $x^3-x-1$
imc-1999-01.body:
Let $p(x)=x^3-x-1$.

**a)** $p$ is a real cubic, so it has a real root $\lambda$. Then $A=\lambda I$ satisfies $A^3-A-I=(\lambda^3-\lambda-1)I=0$.

**b)** *The roots of $p$.* $p'(x)=3x^2-1$, so $p$ has a local maximum at $-\frac1{\sqrt3}$ with value $-\frac1{3\sqrt3}+\frac1{\sqrt3}-1=\frac2{3\sqrt3}-1<0$ and a local minimum at $\frac1{\sqrt3}$ (even smaller). Hence $p<0$ on $(-\infty,\frac1{\sqrt3}]$, $p$ is increasing on $[\frac1{\sqrt3},\infty)$, and $p$ has exactly one real root $\lambda_1$, which is positive. The other two roots are a non-real conjugate pair $\lambda_2,\lambda_3=\overline{\lambda_2}$.

*Eigenvalues of $A$.* If $Av=\mu v$ with $v\ne0$ (over $\mathbb C$), then $0=(A^3-A-I)v=p(\mu)v$, so $p(\mu)=0$. Thus the characteristic polynomial $\chi_A$ (degree $m$, real coefficients) has all its roots among $\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3$. Since $\chi_A$ is real, the non-real roots $\lambda_2,\overline{\lambda_2}$ occur with the same multiplicity $\beta$; let $\alpha$ be the multiplicity of $\lambda_1$. Then
$$\det A=\lambda_1^{\alpha}\,\lambda_2^{\beta}\,\overline{\lambda_2}^{\,\beta}=\lambda_1^{\alpha}\,|\lambda_2|^{2\beta}>0,$$
because $\lambda_1>0$ and $\lambda_2\ne0$. ∎

imc-1999-02.title: Blocks $N+1,\dots,3N$
imc-1999-02.body:
**No.** Let $\pi$ be any bijection of $\mathbb N$ and $N\in\mathbb N$. Among the $2N$ distinct numbers $\pi(N+1),\dots,\pi(3N)$ at most $N$ are $\le N$, so at least $N$ of them are $>N$. Hence
$$\sum_{n=N+1}^{3N}\frac{\pi(n)}{n^2}\ \ge\ \frac1{(3N)^2}\sum_{n=N+1}^{3N}\pi(n)\ >\ \frac1{9N^2}\cdot N\cdot N=\frac19 .$$
This holds for every $N$, so the partial sums of the positive series do not form a Cauchy sequence: the series diverges. ∎

imc-1999-02.title: Summation by parts
imc-1999-02.body:
Let $s_n=\pi(1)+\dots+\pi(n)$. The numbers $\pi(1),\dots,\pi(n)$ are distinct positive integers, so $s_n\ge1+2+\dots+n=\frac{n(n+1)}2$. Abel summation (all terms are positive, so rearranging is fine) gives
$$\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{\pi(n)}{n^2}=\sum_{n=1}^\infty s_n\left(\frac1{n^2}-\frac1{(n+1)^2}\right)\ge\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{n(n+1)}2\cdot\frac{2n+1}{n^2(n+1)^2}=\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{2n+1}{2n(n+1)}\ge\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac1{n+1}=\infty .$$
(To justify the first equality for partial sums: $\sum_{n\le N}\frac{\pi(n)}{n^2}=\sum_{n<N}s_n\bigl(\frac1{n^2}-\frac1{(n+1)^2}\bigr)+\frac{s_N}{N^2}\ge\sum_{n<N}s_n\bigl(\frac1{n^2}-\frac1{(n+1)^2}\bigr)$.) So no such bijection exists. ∎

imc-1999-03.title: Isolate the last term
imc-1999-03.body:
Fix $x,y$ and $n\ge2$. Applying (1) with $n$ and with $n-1$ and using the triangle inequality,
$$3^n\bigl|f(x+ny)-f(x-ny)\bigr|=\left|\sum_{k=1}^n3^k(\dots)-\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}3^k(\dots)\right|\le1+1=2 .$$
(For $n=1$, (1) itself gives $3|f(x+y)-f(x-y)|\le1$.) Hence
$$|f(x+ny)-f(x-ny)|\le\frac2{3^n}\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in\mathbb R,\ n\ge1 .$$
Given any $u,v\in\mathbb R$ and $n\ge1$, choose $x=\frac{u+v}2$ and $y=\frac{v-u}{2n}$, so that $x-ny=u$ and $x+ny=v$. Then $|f(v)-f(u)|\le\frac2{3^n}$ for every $n$; letting $n\to\infty$, $f(u)=f(v)$. So $f$ is constant. ∎

imc-1999-04.title: Iterate along orbits
imc-1999-04.body:
**Check.** For $f(x)=Cx$ ($C>0$): $f\bigl(\frac{x^2}{Cx}\bigr)=f\bigl(\frac xC\bigr)=x$, and $f$ is strictly increasing. We show there are no other solutions.

Let $f$ be a solution and $g(x)=\frac{f(x)}x>0$. The equation shows that $f$ is surjective; being strictly monotone it is injective, so $f$ is a bijection of $(0,\infty)$ and $f^{-1}$ is strictly monotone of the same type. The equation says
$$f^{-1}(x)=\frac{x^2}{f(x)}=\frac x{g(x)} .$$
Then $g\bigl(f^{-1}(x)\bigr)=\dfrac{x}{x/g(x)}=g(x)$, and replacing $x$ by $f(x)$: $g(f(x))=g(x)$. So $g$ is constant along each orbit of $f$.

**Claim:** $f^{(m)}(x)=x\,g(x)^m$ for all $m\in\mathbb Z$ (with $f^{(-m)}=(f^{-1})^{(m)}$). For $m=0,1,-1$ this is clear. If it holds for $m\ge1$, then $f^{(m+1)}(x)=f^{(m)}(x)\,g\bigl(f^{(m)}(x)\bigr)=x\,g(x)^m\cdot g(x)$, using the invariance of $g$ on orbits; the negative direction is identical with $f^{-1}(z)=z/g(z)$.

**$g$ is constant.** $f^{(2)}=f\circ f$ is strictly increasing (a composition of two strictly increasing or two strictly decreasing maps), and so is $f^{(2m)}$ for every $m\in\mathbb Z$. Suppose $0<a<b$ and $g(a)\ne g(b)$. Then for all $m\in\mathbb Z$,
$$a\,g(a)^{2m}<b\,g(b)^{2m},\quad\text{i.e.}\quad \left(\frac{g(a)}{g(b)}\right)^{2m}<\frac ba .$$
If $g(a)/g(b)>1$, let $m\to+\infty$; if $g(a)/g(b)<1$, let $m\to-\infty$. In both cases the left side tends to $+\infty$ — a contradiction. Hence $g\equiv C$ is constant, $C>0$, and $f(x)=Cx$.

**Answer: $f(x)=Cx$ for an arbitrary constant $C>0$.** ∎

imc-1999-05.title: A cycle in the row–column graph
imc-1999-05.body:
Build a bipartite graph $G$: its vertices are the $n$ rows and the $n$ columns; join row $r$ and column $c$ by an edge iff the cell $(r,c)$ is marked. $G$ has $2n$ vertices and $2n$ edges, and no multiple edges.

**$G$ contains a cycle.** A graph without cycles (a forest) on $N$ vertices has at most $N-1$ edges: a forest with at least one edge has a vertex of degree $1$ (the end of a longest path), and deleting it removes one vertex and one edge, so induction on $N$ works. Since $G$ has $2n>2n-1$ edges, it has a cycle.

Because $G$ is bipartite and simple, the cycle has even length $2k$ with $k\ge2$; write it as
$$r_1,c_1,r_2,c_2,\dots,r_k,c_k,(r_1),$$
with distinct rows $r_i$ and distinct columns $c_i$; the edges are $r_ic_i$ and $c_ir_{i+1}$ (indices mod $k$), i.e. the marked cells $P_i=(r_i,c_i)$ and $Q_i=(r_{i+1},c_i)$. Take
$$a_1=Q_k=(r_1,c_k),\ a_2=P_1,\ a_3=Q_1,\ a_4=P_2,\ \dots,\ a_{2k-1}=Q_{k-1},\ a_{2k}=P_k .$$
Then $a_{2i-1}=Q_{i-1}=(r_i,c_{i-1})$ and $a_{2i}=P_i=(r_i,c_i)$ share row $r_i$; $a_{2i}=P_i$ and $a_{2i+1}=Q_i=(r_{i+1},c_i)$ share column $c_i$; finally $a_{2k}=(r_k,c_k)$ and $a_1=(r_1,c_k)$ share column $c_k$. The $2k$ points are distinct because they are distinct edges of the cycle, and $k>1$. ∎

imc-1999-05.title: Delete sparse lines, then walk
imc-1999-05.body:
We prove more generally: if at least $p+q$ cells of a $p\times q$ grid are marked, the required configuration exists.

Delete any row or column containing at most one marked point; this lowers $p+q$ by $1$ and the number of marked points by at most $1$, so the hypothesis persists. Repeat until every remaining row and column contains at least two marked points. The grid never becomes empty: a grid with a single row has at most $q<1+q$ cells, so the invariant "at least $p+q$ marked points" forces at least two rows and two columns at every stage.

Now walk: start at a marked point $b_1$, let $b_2$ be another marked point in its row, $b_3$ another marked point in the column of $b_2$, and so on, alternating row and column moves. By finiteness some point repeats; let $b_m=b_l$ ($l<m$) be the first repetition. If $m-l$ is even, $b_l,\dots,b_{m-1}$ (started at a row step or shifted by one) is an alternating closed sequence of distinct points. If $m-l$ is odd, $b_{l}=b_m$, $b_{l+1}$ and $b_{m-1}$ lie on one line, so dropping $b_l$ and joining $b_{m-1}$ directly to $b_{l+1}$ gives an alternating closed sequence of even length $m-l-1$. A closed alternating sequence needs at least $4$ points (two points in the same row are not in the same column), so $k\ge2$. ∎

imc-1999-06.title: Maximal inequality; an explicit counterexample for $p=1$
imc-1999-06.body:
Write $g=\max(f',0)$ and $h=\max(-f',0)$, so $f'=g-h$, $|f'|=g+h$.

**a)** We show that $c=c_p=\frac{6p}{p-1}$ works. Since $0<f(1)-f(-1)=\int_{-1}^1g-\int_{-1}^1h$, we get
$$\int_{-1}^1|f'|=\int g+\int h<2\int_{-1}^1g,\qquad \int_{-1}^1 g>0. \tag{i}$$
Suppose, for contradiction, that for every $x$ with $f'(x)>0$ there is $y_x\in[-1,1]$ with $|f(y_x)-f(x)|>c\,f'(x)^{1/p}|y_x-x|$ (so $y_x\ne x$).

*Covering lemma.* Let $\varphi=|f'|$ on $[-1,1]$ and $\varphi=0$ outside, and $\lambda>0$. If $E\subseteq[-1,1]$ is open in $[-1,1]$ and each $x\in E$ lies in a nondegenerate interval $I_x$ with $\int_{I_x}\varphi>\lambda|I_x|$, then $|E|\le\frac3\lambda\int\varphi$. Proof: enlarging $I_x$ slightly keeps the strict inequality and makes $x$ an interior point, so we may take $I_x$ open. For a compact $K\subseteq E$ finitely many $I_x$ cover $K$. Select greedily: take the longest, discard all intervals meeting it, repeat. The chosen intervals $I_1,\dots,I_s$ are disjoint, and every discarded interval lies in the concentric interval of triple length of a chosen one that is at least as long; hence $|K|\le3\sum|I_j|<\frac3\lambda\sum\int_{I_j}\varphi\le\frac3\lambda\int\varphi$. Taking the supremum over compact $K\subseteq E$ gives the claim.

*Level sets.* For $t\in(0,1]$ let $E_t=\{x:g(x)>t\}$, open in $[-1,1]$. For $x\in E_t$ the interval $I_x$ between $x$ and $y_x$ satisfies $\int_{I_x}\varphi\ge|f(y_x)-f(x)|>c\,t^{1/p}|I_x|$. By the lemma and (i),
$$|E_t|\le\frac{3}{c\,t^{1/p}}\int|f'|<\frac{6}{c\,t^{1/p}}\int_{-1}^1g\qquad(0<t\le1)$$
(if $E_t=\varnothing$ the strict bound holds trivially since $\int g>0$). Since $0\le g\le1$, the layer-cake formula gives
$$\int_{-1}^1g=\int_0^1|E_t|\,dt<\frac6c\int_{-1}^1g\int_0^1t^{-1/p}\,dt=\frac6c\cdot\frac p{p-1}\int_{-1}^1g=\int_{-1}^1g,$$
a contradiction. Hence $c_p=\frac{6p}{p-1}$ has the required property.

**b) No.** It suffices to refute every $c\ge1$ (a smaller constant is a stronger statement). Fix $c\ge1$, choose $0<\beta<\frac1c$, and a small $x_1>0$ such that $\bigl(\frac{1+x_1}{2x_1}\bigr)^{-\beta}<\frac14$. Put $D=\frac34x_1$ and
$$q(x)=\frac{2\beta D}{x+x_1}\left(\frac{x+x_1}{2x_1}\right)^{-\beta},\qquad H_q(x)=2D\left(\frac{x+x_1}{2x_1}\right)^{-\beta}\quad(x\ge x_1),$$
so that $H_q(x_1)=2D$, $H_q'=-q$ and $q(x)(x+x_1)=\beta H_q(x)$. Note $0<q\le q(x_1)=\frac{\beta D}{x_1}<1$. For $L>0$ define $g_L$ on $[0,1]$ by: $-1$ on $[0,\frac{x_1}2]$, linear from $-1$ to $0$ on $[\frac{x_1}2,x_1]$, and $\min\bigl(L(x-x_1),q(x)\bigr)$ on $[x_1,1]$; it is continuous with $|g_L|\le1$ and $\int_0^{x_1}g_L=-\frac{x_1}2-\frac{x_1}4=-D$. As $L\to\infty$, $\int_{x_1}^1g_L\to\int_{x_1}^1q=2D-H_q(1)>2D-\frac{2D}4>D$ (monotone convergence); fix $L$ with $\int_{x_1}^1g_L>D$. Extend $g=g_L$ evenly to $[-1,1]$ and let $f(x)=\int_0^xg$, an odd $C^1$ function with $|f'|\le1$ and $f(1)=-D+\int_{x_1}^1g>0$, so $f(1)>f(-1)=-f(1)$.

We have $f'(x)>0$ exactly for $|x|>x_1$. Let $x>x_1$ and $y=-x_1$; note $f(x_1)=-D$, $f(-x_1)=D$. Put $H(x)=D-f(x)=2D-\int_{x_1}^xg$. Since $g\le q$ on $[x_1,1]$, $H(x)\ge H_q(x)>0$, so
$$|f(y)-f(x)|=H(x)\ge H_q(x)=\frac{q(x)(x+x_1)}\beta>c\,q(x)(x+x_1)\ge c\,f'(x)\,|y-x|,$$
using $c\beta<1$ and $f'(x)=g(x)\le q(x)$. For $x<-x_1$ take $y=x_1$; by oddness of $f$ and evenness of $g$ the same computation applies. Thus no $x$ satisfies the required inequality with constant $c$, and **no constant exists for $p=1$.** ∎

imc-1999-07.title: Anticommutativity
imc-1999-07.body:
For any $x,y\in R$: $0=(x+y)^2=x^2+xy+yx+y^2=xy+yx$, so $xy=-yx$. Applying this repeatedly (and associativity):
$$abc=a(bc)=-(bc)a=-b(ca)=(ca)b=c(ab)=-(ab)c=-abc .$$
Here we used $a(bc)=-(bc)a$, then $b(ca)=-(ca)b$, then $c(ab)=-(ab)c$. Hence $abc+abc=0$. ∎

imc-1999-08.title: Roots of unity filter
imc-1999-08.body:
Let $p_k$ be the probability that the sum is $k$, and $F(x)=\sum_kp_kx^k=\left(\dfrac{x+x^2+\dots+x^6}6\right)^n$ (the throws are independent). With $\varepsilon=e^{2\pi i/5}$, the filter $\frac15\sum_{j=0}^4\varepsilon^{jk}=[5\mid k]$ gives
$$P(5\mid\text{sum})=\sum_kp_{k}[5\mid k]=\frac15\sum_{j=0}^4F(\varepsilon^j).$$
$F(1)=1$. For $j=1,\dots,4$, $\varepsilon^j+\varepsilon^{2j}+\dots+\varepsilon^{5j}=0$ (a full set of 5th roots of unity), so $\varepsilon^j+\dots+\varepsilon^{6j}=\varepsilon^{6j}=\varepsilon^j$ and $F(\varepsilon^j)=\dfrac{\varepsilon^{jn}}{6^n}$. Now $\sum_{j=1}^4\varepsilon^{jn}$ equals $4$ if $5\mid n$ and $-1$ otherwise. Therefore
$$P=\begin{cases}\dfrac15+\dfrac4{5\cdot6^n},&5\mid n,\\[3mm]\dfrac15-\dfrac1{5\cdot6^n},&5\nmid n.\end{cases}$$
(Check $n=1$: $\frac15-\frac1{30}=\frac16$, only the throw $5$.) ∎

imc-1999-08.title: Group the outcomes in fives
imc-1999-08.body:
Consider the $6^n$ equally likely sequences of results. Every sequence other than $66\dots6$ has the form
$$\underbrace{6\dots6}_{k}\,X\,Y_1\dots Y_{n-k-1},\qquad X\in\{1,\dots,5\},$$
with $k$ and $Y_1,\dots,Y_{n-k-1}$ determined by the sequence. Group together the $5$ sequences that differ only in $X$. Within a group the sums run through $5$ consecutive integers, so exactly one is divisible by $5$. The $6^n-1$ sequences other than $6\dots6$ form $\frac{6^n-1}5$ groups, and the sequence $6\dots6$ has sum $6n$, divisible by $5$ iff $5\mid n$. Hence the number of favourable sequences is $\frac{6^n-1}5+1$ if $5\mid n$ and $\frac{6^n-1}5$ otherwise; dividing by $6^n$ gives the same answer:
$$\frac15+\frac4{5\cdot6^n}\ (5\mid n),\qquad\frac15-\frac1{5\cdot6^n}\ (5\nmid n).$$

imc-1999-09.title: A polynomial inequality valid for $x\ge-1$
imc-1999-09.body:
For every $x\ge-1$,
$$x^3-\frac34x+\frac14=(x+1)\Bigl(x-\frac12\Bigr)^2\ge0,$$
as one checks by expanding: $(x+1)(x^2-x+\frac14)=x^3-\frac34x+\frac14$. Summing over $x=x_1,\dots,x_n$:
$$0\le\sum_{i=1}^nx_i^3-\frac34\sum_{i=1}^nx_i+\frac n4=-\frac34\sum_{i=1}^nx_i+\frac n4,$$
so $\sum x_i\le\frac n3$. ∎

*Remark.* Equality requires every $x_i\in\{-1,\frac12\}$; with $a$ values $-1$ and $b$ values $\frac12$, $\sum x_i^3=0$ gives $b=8a$, so equality occurs exactly when $n=9a$ with $a$ of the $x_i$ equal to $-1$ and $8a$ equal to $\frac12$.

(The polynomial is found by looking for the tangent-line bound $x^3\ge\frac34x-\frac14$, which touches $x^3$ at $x=\frac12$ and holds with equality at the endpoint $x=-1$.)

imc-1999-10.title: Force a fixed drop on every unit interval
imc-1999-10.body:
Suppose such an $f$ exists. Dividing by $f(x)+y>0$,
$$f(x+y)\le\frac{f(x)^2}{f(x)+y}<f(x),\qquad f(x)-f(x+y)\ge f(x)-\frac{f(x)^2}{f(x)+y}=\frac{f(x)\,y}{f(x)+y}. \tag{$*$}$$
In particular $f$ is strictly decreasing.

Fix $x>0$ and choose $n\in\mathbb N$ with $nf(x+1)\ge1$. For $k=0,\dots,n-1$ apply $(*)$ at the point $x_k=x+\frac kn$ with $y=\frac1n$:
$$f(x_k)-f(x_{k+1})\ge\frac{f(x_k)}{nf(x_k)+1}\ge\frac1{2n},$$
because $t\mapsto\frac t{nt+1}$ is increasing and $f(x_k)\ge f(x+1)\ge\frac1n$, so the value is at least $\frac{1/n}{2}$. Adding these $n$ inequalities, $f(x)-f(x+1)\ge\frac12$.

This holds for every $x>0$, so $f(x+m)\le f(x)-\frac m2$ for all $m\in\mathbb N$. Taking $m>2f(x)$ gives $f(x+m)<0$, contradicting $f>0$. Hence no such function exists. ∎

imc-1999-11.title: Absorb the middle of the word
imc-1999-11.body:
By (i) and (ii), any factor $vv$ inside a word can be replaced by $v$: $pvvq\sim pvq$. Below, $w$ may be the empty word (then $uvw$ means $uv$), and empty outer factors are simply omitted.

**Lemma.** If $u$ contains each of the letters $x,y,z$ and $v$ is any word, there is a word $w$ with $uvw\sim u$.

*Proof.* If $v$ is a single letter, say $x$, write $u=u_1xu_2$; then $u\,x\,u_2=u_1(xu_2)(xu_2)\sim u_1xu_2=u$, so $w=u_2$ works. In general let $v=a_1a_2\cdots a_k$ (letters). Each word $ua_1\cdots a_j$ still contains all letters, so by the single-letter case there are words $w_1,\dots,w_k$ with
$$ua_1w_1\sim u,\quad (ua_1)a_2w_2\sim ua_1,\quad\dots,\quad (ua_1\cdots a_{k-1})a_kw_k\sim ua_1\cdots a_{k-1}.$$
Multiplying on the right by (ii) and chaining:
$$uv\,w_kw_{k-1}\cdots w_1\sim ua_1\cdots a_{k-1}\,w_{k-1}\cdots w_1\sim\dots\sim ua_1w_1\sim u .$$
So $w=w_k\cdots w_1$ works. $\square$

**Main argument.** We show that every word $a$ of length $\ge9$ is equivalent to a shorter word; by induction, every word is then equivalent to one of length $\le8$.

If $a$ contains a factor $vv$, then $a\sim$ (the word with $vv$ replaced by $v$), which is shorter. So assume $a$ is *square-free*. Write $a=bcd$ where $b$ and $d$ are the first and last four letters ($c$ is nonempty). A square-free word of length $4$ contains all three letters: over two letters, say $x,y$, every word of length $4$ contains a square (avoiding $xx,yy$ forces alternation $xyxy$ or $yxyx$, which are squares). So $b$ and $d$ contain all of $x,y,z$.

By the Lemma there is $e$ with $b(cd)e\sim b$, and then $f$ with $d\,e\,f\sim d$. Now
$$a=bcd\ \sim\ bc(def)\ \sim\ bc(de)(de)f\ =\ (bcde)(def)\ \sim\ b(def)\ \sim\ bd,$$
using $d\sim def$, then $(de)(de)\sim de$, then $bcde\sim b$, then $def\sim d$ (each time with (ii)). The word $bd$ has length $8<|a|$. ∎

imc-1999-12.title: Pigeonhole on the torus
imc-1999-12.body:
(We assume $n\ge2$, so that some $r\ne0$ exists.) Let $A=\{a_1,\dots,a_k\}$. If $k=0$, any $r\ne0$ works. Let $k\ge1$; then $k\le\frac{\ln n}{100}$ gives
$$6^k=e^{k\ln6}\le n^{\ln6/100}<n .$$
Divide the unit circle into $6$ half-open arcs of angle $\frac\pi3$. For $t=0,1,\dots,n-1$ consider the $k$-tuple
$$\Bigl(\exp\tfrac{2\pi ia_1t}n,\ \dots,\ \exp\tfrac{2\pi ia_kt}n\Bigr),$$
and classify it by which arc each coordinate lies in. There are $6^k<n$ classes and $n$ tuples, so two of them, for $t_1<t_2$, are in the same class. Let $r=t_2-t_1\in\{1,\dots,n-1\}$, so $r\ne0$ in $\mathbb Z_n$. For each $j$, the points $\exp\frac{2\pi ia_jt_1}n$ and $\exp\frac{2\pi ia_jt_2}n$ lie on a common arc of angle $\frac\pi3$, so the angle between them is less than $\frac\pi3$ and
$$\operatorname{Re}\exp\frac{2\pi ia_jr}n=\cos\Bigl(\frac{2\pi a_jt_2}n-\frac{2\pi a_jt_1}n\Bigr)>\cos\frac\pi3=\frac12 .$$
Summing over $j$,
$$|f(r)|\ge\operatorname{Re}f(r)>\frac k2=\frac{|A|}2.\ \blacksquare$$
